items.definition: To take a matter to a more senior person because it has not moved.
items.example: If we do not hear back by Friday, we will need to escalate this.

items.definition: To give formal permission for something to go ahead.
items.example: Legal has green-lighted the launch for June.

items.definition: The closing line of an email, such as "Kind regards", followed by your name.
items.example: Use a plain sign-off: Kind regards, then your name and title.

items.definition: Agreement and active support for a plan from the people who must carry it out.
items.example: I spent two weeks getting buy-in from the regional teams.

items.definition: A force working against you, such as a rule change or a weak market.
items.example: We are facing a headwind from the new import regulations.

items.definition: The easy results, available with little effort before the harder work.
items.example: We picked the low-hanging fruit first and delivered in three weeks.

items.definition: To increase activity, output or capability, often over a planned period.
items.example: We are ramping up production ahead of the festival season.

items.definition: A long, detailed examination of one subject.
items.example: We did a deep dive on the churn numbers before the review.

items.definition: A rough approximate number, given before the real figure is known.
items.example: Could you give me a ballpark figure for the full build?

items.definition: The capacity a person or team has to take on more work.
items.example: I do not have the bandwidth this week, but I can do it next month.

items.definition: One of the ways your body finds out about the world. You have five main ones.
items.example: Smell is a sense that helps you find food.

items.definition: The screen at the back of your eye. Light lands on it and the picture begins.
items.example: The picture forms on the retina.

items.definition: The nerve that carries the picture from your eye to your brain.
items.example: The optic nerve carries the picture along to the brain.

items.definition: The little spiral inside your ear that turns vibrations into nerve signals.
items.example: The cochlea changes the movement of your eardrum into signals.

items.definition: The tiny bumps on your tongue that pick out sweet, salty, sour and bitter.
items.example: Taste buds tell you that the mango is sweet.

items.definition: The cable that carries messages inside your body, from the senses to the brain and back again.
items.example: A nerve carries the message from your finger to your brain.

items.definition: Doing a calculation in your head, without a calculator and without paper.
items.example: Mental arithmetic gave me the rough figure, and the check gave me the right one.

items.definition: A rough number, close enough to show whether a real answer is possible.
items.example: Before you multiply, estimate: about 50 times about 30 is about 1500.

items.definition: Writing a number as the nearest convenient value, usually the nearest ten, hundred or thousand.
items.example: 47 rounds to 50, and 42 rounds to 40.

items.definition: The correction you add or subtract after you have rounded a number.
items.example: I rounded 19 up to 20, so the compensation is one lot of 24, and 480 − 24 = 456.

items.definition: To bear or transport something.
items.example: In 8 + 7 you write 5 and carry 1 to the next column.

items.definition: The part of a number that is left over when the division does not come out exactly.
items.example: 87 divided by 7 gives the quotient 12 and the remainder 3.

items.definition: The result of a division, without the part that is left over.
items.example: The quotient of 87 and 7 is 12, with a remainder of 3.

items.definition: The total of all the digits of a number, used to test whether it is a multiple of 9.
items.example: The digit sum of 1296 is 1 + 2 + 9 + 6 = 18, a multiple of 9.

items.definition: A period in which investment and valuations in AI exceed the technology's near-term economic value.
The observed pattern in which new technologies pass through inflated expectations, disappointment, and eventual steady adoption.
The total price investors place on a company or sector, reflecting expected future profits rather than current ones.
The historical lag between the arrival of a transformative technology and its measurable effect on economic productivity.
The investigation of claims, numbers and risks before committing money or reputation.
The revenue and cost attached to one unit of a product — the arithmetic of whether a business model works.
The pattern in which removing difficulty lowers the tolerance for difficulty, making life feel harder even as it gets easier.
The capacity to recover quickly and fully after stress, failure or loss.
Sustained effort toward long-term goals, maintained through boredom and setbacks.
The property of growing stronger under stress and disorder, beyond mere resistance to damage.
The willingness to give up a smaller reward now for a larger reward later.
The small resistance between wanting something and getting it, which slows consumption and quietly trains patience.
items.example: Every plan met friction: the weather, the delay, the wrong order.

items.definition: The false feeling of competence that comes from producing results with powerful tools rather than from owned ability.
Results and confidence produced by tools, which the user experiences as personal ability.
The systematic tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one's own knowledge and the odds of one's success.
The tendency to trust automated systems more than one's own judgment, especially under pressure or fatigue.
